From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s unified corporate banking portal. Alongside the build, Matt led payments data migration without disruption to live payment operations. He translated regional regulatory requirements into data visibility and access controls, sequencing launches by regulatory readiness rather than a single global deployment. He also owned production incident response and cross-team root-cause analysis.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a portal serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**. Client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories were preserved through the migration.

answer_md:
🐾 Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose.

He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His response was to remove those barriers: make intent explicit, create psychological safety so people could speak honestly, and push decisions to the people closest to the work. At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, that included a “permit to fail” learning environment. When fear of blame kept teams from experimenting, Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. Teams applied lessons to subsequent sprints rather than pointing fingers when something went wrong.

In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail, intentionally. Instead of treating polished requirements and predictable outcomes as prerequisites, teams used user research, Jobs to Be Done framing, and rapid testing to validate assumptions before committing to costly builds. Failed experiments became decision inputs rather than setbacks.

He also assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, automation, and continuous delivery were part of daily work, alongside direct feedback and open communication.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops. Matt’s stated non-negotiables include integrity and respect, continuous learning, and “outcomes, not optics.”

APIs, microservices, change data capture, and reconciliation connected the new platform to the existing system of record. When the client grew restless for tangible progress, he brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create through weekly build-measure-learn iterations. The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. Client contributors paired into the build and learned the technologies needed to support the application themselves.

Matt also built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, owning full P&L accountability, hiring, training, and career development. question: Why hire Matt?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying the IAM configuration and downstream access controls, he assumed the inherited setup was correct. He focused on delivery pressures, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. Compensating controls, such as data masking and email interception, were not in place.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Following the incident, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed on a platform delivery.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying those controls, he assumed they were correct. He focused on delivery pressures, relied on inherited documentation, and did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project: a systemic failure resulted in an individual consequence.

Matt’s stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach, rather than inherited conditions he assumed were already correct.

🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs weren’t keeping pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured program that would help engineers earn certifications and prepare them to lead cloud-native transformation initiatives.

From **July 2018** to **November 2019**, Matt led AWS Launchpad, developed in collaboration with AWS. Rather than relying on theory alone, he built the program around structured learning paths, hands-on labs, and mentor-based training.

He designed learning paths and certification programs covering AWS core services and cloud-native application development. Topics included Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate. Interactive workshops put engineers into real-world AWS environments so they could apply what they were learning.

Matt also established cloud expert mentorship teams to embed AWS best practices and retain knowledge across the organization. He organized group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops, giving participants support beyond the training materials. The program combined a defined path toward certification with practical exercises, expert guidance, and peer learning.

More than **200 professionals earned AWS certifications**, including AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications. The program accelerated AWS adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives across **Accenture**.

Matt later coordinated a separate AWS training track for **Accenture’s** annual ARISE HBCU Conference, assembling curriculum, presenters, and keynote speakers, personally teaching cloud fundamentals, and coordinating free AWS certificate training opportunities. That program reached more than **250 students and recent graduates each year** from **2020** through **2023**.
